notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Jeremiah 10, drawing from the sourced material across multiple traditions.

---

## Jeremiah 10 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter falls into two main parts: (1) a sustained contrast between the living God and worthless idols (vv. 1–16), and (2) a prophecy of coming judgment followed by Jeremiah’s lament and prayer (vv. 17–25). Several commentators note that vv. 1–16 appear to be a distinct unit — possibly even a parenthesis — before Jeremiah returns to his theme of the Babylonian invasion (Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary).

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm

---

### v. 1 — “Hear the word that the LORD speaks to you, O house of Israel.”

This verse forms the link to the previous chapter, where Israel was described as “uncircumcised in heart” and on a level with the heathen. Now the special sin of the heathen — idolatry — is set forth. God addresses the whole “house of Israel,” including the already exiled northern kingdom, warning them against the religious customs of the nations. The Hebrew verb for “learn” (*tilmadu*) can carry the sense of “becoming a disciple”; God is warning them not to become disciples of pagan religions.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 2 — “Do not learn the ways of the nations or be terrified by the signs in the heavens…”

The “signs of the heavens” refer not to the normal sun, moon, and stars (Genesis 1:14) but to unusual phenomena — eclipses, comets, meteors, and planetary conjunctions — which the Chaldeans and other nations interpreted astrologically as portents of disaster (Feinberg; Ellicott). The Chaldeans in particular were devoted to judicial astrology (Isaiah 47:13). God’s people are told not to share the superstitious dread of the nations, because Yahweh controls even the heavens. The fear of heavenly signs is described as a “Heathenish fear.”

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-10.html (Constable)

---

### v. 3 — “For the customs of the peoples are worthless; they cut down a tree from the forest…”

The word translated “customs” is better rendered “statutes” or “ordinances” — referring specifically to religious rites, not general cultural habits (Ellicott; Gill). The prophet mocks the process: a tree is cut from the forest, shaped by a craftsman’s tools, and then worshipped. The sheer ordinariness of the raw material exposes the absurdity of idolatry. Similar mockery of idol-manufacture appears in Isaiah 40:18–20 and 44:9–20. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the passage is so similar to Isaiah’s language that one writer likely saw the other’s work.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-10.html (Pulpit)

---

### v. 4 — “They adorn it with silver and gold and fasten it with hammer and nails, so that it will not totter.”

The idol is plated with precious metals for ornament and nailed down so it will not fall over. Gill notes the irony: without the nails, the “god” could not even keep its own silver and gold decking, let alone help its worshippers. The image is of something that must be secured by its makers — it cannot secure itself.

**The Christmas Tree Debate:** Many readers notice the similarity to the modern Christmas tree: a tree cut down, set up, and decorated. David Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic) treats this at length. He notes several reasons the passage should not be used to prohibit Christmas trees: (1) Jeremiah addressed pagan customs; proper Christmas celebration is an expression of Christian belief, not a custom of unbelievers. (2) Today, an unbeliever with a Christmas tree is borrowing from Christian tradition, not vice versa. (3) The tree in Jeremiah was worshipped as an idol — a modern Christmas tree (properly understood) is not. (4) Jeremiah wrote in a context where trees were directly connected to idolatry (cf. Jeremiah 2:27). Guzik adds that if a Christian’s conscience is troubled, they should follow Romans 14:23 (“whatever is not from faith is sin”) and abstain.

GotQuestions.org (evangelical) states flatly: “There is nothing in the Bible that either commands or prohibits Christmas trees… unless we bow down before our Christmas tree, carve it into an idol, and pray to it, these passages cannot be applied to Christmas trees.”

Catholic Answers likewise argues: “Jeremiah was not talking about Christmas trees. He was writing hundreds of years before Christmas became a celebration… Christians are not intent on worshipping their trees.”

Desiring God (John Piper, Reformed Baptist) notes that the passage is “an implicit warning to believers of all ages never to turn away from the living God to a created thing… and treat it as an object of greater affection to you than you have in the living God,” but does not use it to ban Christmas trees.

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://www.gotquestions.org/Christmas-tree.html ; https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/refuting-the-pagan-roots-of-christmas-claim ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 5 — “Like scarecrows in a cucumber patch, their idols cannot speak…”

The Hebrew is difficult; it can be rendered either “upright like a palm tree” (KJV/NKJV) or “like a scarecrow in a cucumber field” (NASB/ESV). The scarecrow image — a stiff, immobile figure that only frightens birds — emphasizes impotence. Idols cannot speak to command, counsel, or comfort. They must be carried; they cannot walk. The climax: “Do not fear them, for they can do no harm, and neither can they do any good.” They are, as Constable puts it, “do-nothing gods.” The apocryphal “Epistle of Jeremiah” (in Baruch) uses the same scarecrow comparison, suggesting this was the accepted ancient understanding.

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-10.html (Constable) ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 6 — “There is none like You, O LORD. You are great, and Your name is mighty in power.”

The tone shifts abruptly from mocking idols to praising Yahweh. The Hebrew opens with a vigorous abruptness: “None is there like Thee, O LORD” (Ellicott). Gill notes that there is none like Him “for the perfections of his nature, for the works of his hands, and for the instances of his kindness.” His “name” represents His revealed character, and it is “great in might” — a term used elsewhere for divine omnipotence (cf. Isaiah 9:6, “Mighty God”).

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 7 — “Who would not fear You, O King of nations? This is Your due.”

God is here called “King of nations” (or “King of the heathen”) — a title expressing His universal sovereignty, in deliberate contrast to the notion that He is God of the Jews only (Ellicott; cf. Romans 3:29). Fear — reverent awe — is His rightful due. Among all the wise men and all the kingdoms, none compares to Him. Gill: even the wisest kings and counsellors of the nations have no wisdom, glory, or kingdom like His.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 8 — “But they are altogether senseless and foolish, instructed by worthless idols made of wood!”

“Altogether” is literally “in one” — meaning “in one thing they are brutish,” namely idolatry (Gill; Ellicott). The phrase “a wooden idol is a worthless doctrine” (BSB: “instructed by worthless idols made of wood”) can be rendered: “the instruction of vanities is the tree itself” — meaning the teaching received from idols has no more value than the wood from which they are made (Harrison, cited by Guzik).

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm

---

### v. 9 — “Hammered silver is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz…”

The raw materials are imported at great cost: silver from Tarshish (probably Tartessus in Spain, the western limit of the ancient world) and gold from Uphaz (possibly a variant of Ophir, or a term for “refined gold”). The idol is dressed in blue and purple — the most precious dyes, associated with royalty and the tabernacle. All this artistry is “the work of skilled men.” The implied contrast: the more expense and skill poured into the idol, the more shameful that it is worshipped. “Men make idols. Jehovah makes men” (G. Campbell Morgan, cited by Guzik).

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 10 — “But the LORD is the true God; He is the living God and eternal King.”

This verse contains a concentrated statement of who Yahweh is. The Hebrew reads literally: “Jehovah is the God that is Truth” — truth in its highest, most perfect form (Ellicott). St. John uses the same Greek word (*alēthinos*) in John 17:3 and 1 John 5:20. He is “the living God” — the Hebrew is plural (*elohim hayyim*, “living Gods”), which Gill notes may hint at the plurality of Persons in the Godhead, while the singular “He” (*hu*) preserves the unity. “Eternal King” is literally “King of Eternity,” far grander than “everlasting king.” At His wrath, the earth trembles and the nations cannot endure — something no idol can do.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/

---

### v. 11 — “Thus you are to tell them: ‘These gods… will perish from this earth and from under these heavens.’”

This is the only verse in the entire book of Jeremiah written in Aramaic (Chaldee), not Hebrew. Two explanations are offered: (1) it was a marginal note by an exile in Babylon that later entered the text, or (2) — the view Ellicott and most commentators prefer — the prophet deliberately put into the mouths of the exiles the very words they were to use when invited to worship Babylonian gods. It has the ring of a popular proverb. In the original there is a play on words: “the gods that have not *made*… shall be *made away with*.” The Aramaic form gave it the character of a public confession in the language of the captors. Feinberg notes that though some critics reject the verse as a gloss, all ancient versions include it and it fits the context perfectly.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 12 — “The LORD made the earth by His power; He established the world by His wisdom…”

The verbs are participial in Hebrew — “making… establishing… stretching out” — presenting God’s creative activity as ongoing and characteristic of Him (Ellicott). The “test between idols and Jehovah,” writes G. Campbell Morgan, “is the test of creation.” The idols made nothing; Yahweh made everything. “World” (*tebel*) here refers specifically to the inhabited, productive world in its relation to humanity, as distinct from the material earth (*erets*).

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/

---

### v. 13 — “When He thunders, the waters in the heavens roar…”

The prophet finds evidence of God’s power both in the fixed order of creation and in its dramatic disruptions. Thunder is pictured as God’s voice (cf. Psalm 29:3); it brings a “rush of waters” in the heavens. He causes vapours to rise, makes lightning for the rain, and brings wind from His storehouses. The second half of this verse agrees verbally with Psalm 135:7 — one is a quotation from the other or both draw on a common source (Ellicott). The “treasuries” of wind echo Job 38:22.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 14 — “Every man is senseless and devoid of knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols.”

The Hebrew reads “brutish from knowing” — i.e., too brutish to know, or brutish for lack of knowledge (Ellicott). The smelter who pours molten metal into a mold is shamed by his own creation: “his molten image is falsehood, and there is no breath in them.” The idol is a lie — it promises what it cannot deliver. Gill: “there is no breath in them; they are mere stocks and stones, lifeless and inanimate.”

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/

---

### v. 15 — “They are worthless, a work to be mocked. In the time of their punishment they will perish.”

“A work of errors” is better translated “a work of mockery” — worthy only of derision (Ellicott; Feinberg). “In the time of their visitation” means the time when God visits them with punishment (cf. 1 Peter 2:12; Isaiah 10:3). Both the idols and their makers will perish together in the day of judgment (Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary).

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 16 — “The Portion of Jacob is not like these, for He is the Maker of all things…”

“The Portion of Jacob” is a beautiful title: God Himself is the inheritance and treasure of His people (cf. Psalm 16:5; 119:57). He is “the Maker of all things” — literally “the Former of the all,” i.e., of the universe (Ellicott). “Israel is the tribe of His inheritance” — the phrase “rod of his inheritance” (KJV) may mean “sceptre,” indicating that Israel is the people over whom and through whom God rules. The chapter’s doxology climaxes with the majestic name “the LORD of Hosts” (*Yahweh Sabaoth*) — the Lord of the armies of heaven, the stars, the angels, and the armies of Israel — a name no pagan deity could match.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 17 — “Gather up your belongings from this land, you who live under siege.”

The long parenthesis on idolatry (vv. 1–16) ends; Jeremiah returns to his main theme of coming judgment. The “inhabitant of the fortress” (KJV) is a feminine noun — the daughter of Zion, sitting in a besieged city, told to gather her goods into one small bundle for exile. Ellicott suggests the phrase has a proverbial ring, like “bag and baggage.” The Hebrew word for “wares” may refer simply to a travelling carpet or mantle.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 18 — “Behold, at this time I will sling out the inhabitants of the land…”

“I will sling out” is a vivid metaphor: God will hurl the inhabitants out of the land as from a sling — fast, hard, and far. Trapp comments: “I will easily and speedily sling them, and sling them into Babylon; so God will one day hurl into hell all the wicked of the earth.” The final phrase “that they may be captured” (BSB; KJV “that they may find it so”) is an abrupt Hebrew construction. Ellicott notes the ellipsis may be intentional: “they would find…” — what they found would depend on themselves. Some versions (Syriac) supply “me,” meaning “that they may find Me” — i.e., be led through misery to seek God (cf. Deuteronomy 4:29; Jeremiah 29:13).

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 19 — “Woe to me because of my brokenness; my wound is grievous! But I said, ‘This is truly my sickness, and I must bear it.’”

The prophet now speaks in the voice of Jerusalem personified — a mother lamenting her wound. The phrase “this is my grief” (or “my sickness”) indicates she recognizes that the calamity is self-inflicted; she must bear what she has brought on herself. Accepting the punishment is the first step toward repentance (Ellicott). The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes that “her wound is grievous, but she realizes that she must bear it” (cf. Micah 7:9).

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-10.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/

---

### v. 20 — “My tent is destroyed, and all its ropes are snapped. My sons have departed from me and are no more.”

The destruction of the city is pictured as the collapse of a tent: the covering is spoiled, the cords are broken, and the children who used to help their mother pitch the tent and set up its curtains are dead or exiled. Cundall: “Jerusalem is personified as a tent-dwelling mother, bereft of her children.” The tent imagery is significant — the daughter of Zion is reduced to her ancient nomadic state.

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 21 — “For the shepherds have become senseless; they do not seek the LORD. Therefore they have not prospered, and all their flock is scattered.”

The “shepherds” (or “pastors”) are the rulers of Judah — kings, priests, prophets, counsellors — not priests alone (Ellicott; cf. Jeremiah 2:8; 3:15). Their fundamental failure was that they “did not seek the LORD” — they were prayerless. “Therefore they have not prospered” is more accurately “therefore they have not done wisely” (Ellicott). F. B. Meyer, cited by Guzik, says: “it is incontestable that a dwindling flock and waning cause point to prayerlessness perhaps on the part of the members, but almost certainly on the part of the shepherd himself.”

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 22 — “Listen! The sound of a report is coming— a great commotion from the land to the north.”

The “north country” is Babylon (cf. Jeremiah 1:13–14). Ellicott renders it: “A cry is heard, Behold, it cometh” — a cry of terror, terrible in its brevity, announcing the invading army. The result: the cities of Judah become “a desolation, a haunt for jackals” (KJV “a den of dragons”). The word “bruit” (KJV) is an obsolete English word for “rumour” or “report.”

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 23 — “I know, O LORD, that a man’s way is not his own; no one who walks directs his own steps.”

This is one of the most-quoted verses in the chapter. The confession is made by the prophet on behalf of Israel (Ellicott). The two Hebrew words for “man” are different: the first (*adam*) stresses weakness and earthiness; the second (*geber*) denotes strength. Even the strong man cannot direct his own steps — he needs divine guidance.

**Spurgeon’s sermon on this verse** (“An Instructive Truth,” June 22, 1876) draws out several lessons: (1) The truth was Jeremiah’s consolation amid the Babylonian crisis: “Nebuchadnezzar was about to carry the Jews away… but the prophet consoled himself with the reflection that, whatever Nebuchadnezzar meant to do, he was only the instrument in the hands of God.” (2) This truth should banish fear of man — even the mightiest are under God’s control. (3) It should produce submission to God’s will: “A dog, when he is struck with a stick, usually bites the stick… your contention must not be against the instrument of your affliction.” (4) Man ought not to direct his own way because his will is naturally evil: “He who is his own guide is guided by a fool.” (5) There is One who will direct our steps — we may abandon our own choosings and say, “Not as I will, but as Thou wilt.”

**David Guzik** (Enduring Word, Pentecostal) adds that the verse reflects deep trust in God’s sovereignty: even the Babylonians’ steps are directed by God.

The Preacher’s Complete Homiletical Commentary notes that “a Divine direction and determination overrule our planning.”

**Sources:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/jeremiah-10.html (Spurgeon excerpt) ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 24 — “Correct me, O LORD, but only with justice— not in Your anger, or You will bring me to nothing.”

Jeremiah does not ask to escape correction — he knows Judah must be disciplined. But he pleads for God to correct “with justice” (or “in measure,” as the same Hebrew word is translated in Jeremiah 30:11 and 46:28). The request is for measured, reformative discipline, not vindictive, annihilating wrath. “Lest Thou bring me to nothing” is literally “lest Thou make me small.” The prophet stands as representative of the nation, pleading for mercy in the midst of deserved judgment.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-10.html

---

### v. 25 — “Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You… for they have devoured Jacob.”

This verse is virtually identical to Psalm 79:6–7. Ellicott judges it more probable that the Psalmist borrowed from the prophet. Jeremiah asks that the fury of God be poured on the nations that served as His instrument of judgment on Judah — because they “do not know” God, “do not call on” His name, and have “devoured Jacob” with excessive cruelty. Spurgeon comments: “Knowing what we do about the Babylonians, we do not wonder that Jeremiah put up such a prayer as that.” Clarke adds that this was fulfilled: “Nebuchadnezzar was punished with madness, his son was slain… and the Babylonish empire was finally destroyed.”

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-10.html

---

## Notable Points of Difference Among Traditions

### The Christmas Tree Controversy (vv. 3–4)

Some Christian groups — particularly certain conservative Protestant and Sabbatarian groups — have used Jeremiah 10:3–4 to argue that Christmas trees are a pagan practice condemned by Scripture. The mainstream response across traditions is nearly uniform: the passage condemns idol worship, not seasonal decoration.

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** David Guzik devotes extensive space to the question, concluding that the differences between a pagan idol-tree and a Christmas tree are greater than the similarities, but that those with a tender conscience should follow Romans 14:23.
- **Evangelical (GotQuestions.org):** States plainly that “there is nothing in the Bible that either commands or prohibits Christmas trees” and that application of Jeremiah 10 to Christmas trees is a misreading.
- **Reformed Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper):** Treats the passage as a warning against treating any created thing as an object of ultimate affection, but does not use it to ban Christmas celebrations.
- **Catholic (Catholic Answers):** Notes that the Christmas tree tradition originated with Protestant Christians in 16th-century Germany, centuries after Jeremiah wrote, and that Christians do not worship their trees.
- **Bible.org / Dallas Theological Seminary (The Bible Knowledge Commentary):** Agrees there are only “superficial similarities” and that the tree is “not something we worship as a god.”

**Source:** https://www.gotquestions.org/Christmas-tree.html ; https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/refuting-the-pagan-roots-of-christmas-claim ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/

---

### The Aramaic Verse (v. 11)

Ellicott and Feinberg note that some critical scholars reject v. 11 as a later gloss because it is the only Aramaic verse in Jeremiah. However, Ellicott favours the view that Jeremiah — who had contact with Chaldeans — deliberately used Aramaic to give the exiles a public confession in the language of their captors. All ancient versions include the verse. The traditional reading across Protestant and Catholic traditions accepts its authenticity.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/

---

### Authorship of vv. 1–16

The Pulpit Commentary raises the question of whether vv. 1–16 were actually written by Jeremiah, noting the interruption of the flow between Jeremiah 9 and 10:17–25, and the close stylistic parallels to Isaiah 40–44. The Pulpit commentator suggests the passage may not be Jeremiah’s own work, though “as it forms part of a canonical book, its claims to the character of a Scripture remain the same.” Other traditional commentators (Gill, Ellicott, Henry) treat it without question as Jeremiah’s own prophecy.

**Source:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-10.html (Pulpit)

---

### v. 23 and Divine Sovereignty vs. Human Free Will

This verse is a classic proof-text in discussions of God’s sovereignty. Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist) uses it to show that “the affairs of this world are not under the control of men” and that even wicked rulers like Nebuchadnezzar are instruments in God’s hands — while insisting that “the free agency of man is a self-evident truth.” The Preacher’s Complete Homiletical Commentary applies it to frustrated national policy: Judah’s attempts to negotiate with Assyria, Egypt, and Babylon were futile because God’s purposes overruled them. The verse is cited across traditions (Reformed, Baptist, Pentecostal) with broad agreement that it teaches human dependence on God’s direction, though the emphasis on predestination versus free will varies.

**Sources:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/jeremiah-10.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-10.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/

---

### v. 25 and the Imprecatory Prayer

Jeremiah’s prayer for wrath on the nations mirrors Psalm 79:6–7. Spurgeon comments without apology that given what the Babylonians did, “we do not wonder that Jeremiah put up such a prayer.” This imprecatory element has been debated: some modern readers find it ethically challenging. Traditional commentators (Gill, Clarke, Ellicott) treat it as a legitimate prophetic appeal for divine justice against those who exceeded their mandate as instruments of judgment.

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-10/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/10.htm

---

## Summary

Jeremiah 10 divides into a satirical exposé of idolatry (vv. 1–16) and a prophecy of exile with the prophet’s lament (vv. 17–25). The chapter’s great theological contribution is its contrast between dead idols — manufactured, decorated, carried, and mute — and the living God who made all things, directs human steps, and will judge both His own people and the nations. Across Protestant traditions, there is broad agreement on the chapter’s meaning, with the main point of modern debate being its (mis)application to Christmas trees. The chapter closes with one of Scripture’s most memorable confessions of human dependence on divine sovereignty: “I know, O LORD, that a man’s way is not his own; no one who walks directs his own steps.”
